questions.q: What is the recursive step in recursive reward modeling?
options: Training the same reward model repeatedly on identical data with no changes
Giving a human AI assistants that handle specific sub-components of evaluating a hard task, then repeating this assisted-evaluation-and-train cycle across generations
Having the model evaluate its own outputs with no human involvement at all
Running the debate protocol recursively instead of using reward modeling
questions.explain: The method extends ordinary reward modeling by having AI assistants help the human evaluator, and by repeating that process across rounds of increasing capability.

questions.q: What role do AI assistants play for the human evaluator in this method?
options: They replace the human entirely, removing human judgment from the process
They handle specific sub-components of a complex evaluation, such as summarizing a document or checking a factual claim, extending what the human can reliably judge
They only provide entertainment while the human works on something else
They exist solely to slow down the evaluation process for safety reasons
questions.explain: Assistants extend the human's judgment to sub-tasks the human couldn't fully evaluate unassisted, rather than replacing the human's role.

questions.q: Why is the process described as climbing a "capability ladder" across rounds?
options: Because each round's trained system can become an assistant for evaluating the next, harder round, so oversight capability is meant to climb alongside model capability
Because the models get physically larger with each round of training
Because the ladder refers only to the number of human evaluators hired over time
Because each round uses a completely unrelated reward model with no connection to prior rounds
questions.explain: Round one's output feeding into round two's evaluation process is what lets oversight capability climb the same ladder as model capability, rather than staying fixed.

questions.q: What is the main risk this lesson identifies with recursive reward modeling?
options: That it requires far more compute than any other oversight technique and is therefore impractical
That an assistant's blind spot or error introduced in an early round can get baked into the reward model and compound across later rounds
That it cannot be combined with any form of human feedback
That it only works on tasks that have no correct answer
questions.explain: Because each round builds on the last, an unreliable assistant's errors can propagate and compound rather than staying contained to a single step.

questions.q: How does this lesson describe the relationship between recursive reward modeling's core risk and the scalability ceiling discussed earlier in the course?
options: They are completely unrelated concepts with no connection
It's the same underlying concern relocated — now the question is whether the AI assistants' judgment is reliable, rather than whether an unassisted human's judgment is reliable
Recursive reward modeling has been proven to fully eliminate the scalability ceiling
The scalability ceiling only applies to capability evaluations, never to oversight techniques
questions.explain: The lesson frames this explicitly: the reliance on reliable judgment doesn't disappear, it shifts from the unassisted human to the AI assistants helping that human.
